alt: Three cards sort the criticisms. Structure: isolation and idealisation, loss of functions and lack of contact with kin. Power: the status of women, Zaretsky and Delphy and Leonard. Harm: marital breakdown and dysfunctional families.
caption: Each criticism is about the family’s structure, its power relations or the harm it can do.

after: ## The six criticisms in the specification
alt: A table of the six criticisms: isolation and unrealistic idealisation, loss of traditional functions, lack of contact with wider kin, the status and role of women, marital breakdown and dysfunctional families, each with the problem it names and the writers or perspective behind it.
caption: Name the criticism, explain the problem, and say who makes it.

after: ## The six criticisms in the specification
alt: Left: a family in Bethnal Green surrounded by relatives, with daily contact and help with childcare. Right: after moving to a new estate outside London the family is home-centred and isolated, with kin far away. Below, the counter-argument that the modified extended family keeps in touch by phone, video calls, visits and money.
caption: Moving away from kin made families more home-centred and more isolated.

after: ## Zaretsky: a Marxist view of developments in families
alt: A cycle: a worker in a dull, insecure job comes home to the family, which cushions him, so the job feels bearable and he does not challenge the system; the family spends wages on goods, which returns profit to capitalists. Below, Zaretsky’s points that the private family is an illusion and only socialism would end the problem.
caption: By cushioning workers, the family keeps capitalism going.

after: ## Delphy and Leonard: a feminist critique
alt: A dual-earner couple: both have full-time paid jobs, but the woman also does the cooking, cleaning and organising of the children, and her labour gives the man free time and comfort. Below, Delphy and Leonard’s argument that the family is an economic system in which men exploit women’s work, with criticisms.
caption: For Delphy and Leonard, men, not capitalists, gain from women’s work in the family.

alt: Two panels. Critics say the family is isolated, benefits capitalism or men, places unrealistic demands on couples and can hide harm. Functionalists reply that these are exceptions: most families socialise children and give emotional support, and high divorce may show people value marriage.
caption: Judge whether each criticism applies to all families or only some.
